name: Orange
lede: Orange is the color between red and yellow, named after a fruit: a late arrival as a word, a pigment and an idea, which went on to become the color of princes, monks' robes and every warning sign that needs to be seen.

sections.title: The fruit came first
sections.body:
Orange is named after the fruit, and the fruit's name travelled west with it: Persian *narang*, Arabic *naranj*, Sanskrit *naranga*, Spanish *naranja*, French *orenge*, then English *orange* [1]. Early English said *a narange* [6]. The first letter slid across to the article, the same drift, called aphesis, that turned a napron into an apron and a nadder into an adder [6]. Jarman leaves open whether the fruit or the color came first [7], but St Clair is clear that the fruit name is the older one [1].

As a color word, orange is young. St Clair dates it to the sixteenth century; before that English speakers made do with *giolureade*, yellow-red [1]. One early use is a 1502 purchase by Elizabeth of York of orange-colored sarsenet sleeves for Margaret Tudor [1]. The sources disagree by a decade: Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary gives 1512 as the first record of the color name [40].

Latin had no single word for it either. *Croceus*, the saffron word, leaned toward orange [10]. Pastoureau finds that ancient and medieval writers never made orange a category of its own: orange things were described with the words for [[yellow]], [[brown]] and [[red]], and the hue was often lumped in with *rufus*, a disparaged [[russet]] [8]. Things that now look plainly orange, such as the lead pigment minium, were filed as red or yellow [1][3].

sections.title: How orange became a color
sections.body:
Dyers could always make orange by passing cloth through a red vat and then a yellow one, but medieval results were dull and brownish, and few people asked for them [8]. Rome's dyers' rules already named three trades for orange and yellow, working with safflower, saffron and weld [9]. The change came at the end of the fourteenth century, when brazilwood from South India, Ceylon and Sumatra reached European dyers in quantity [8]. With alkaline mordants it gave pinks, and with acid ones, vinegar or urine, it gave clear oranges [8].

Princes liked the novelty. Pastoureau names Jean de Berry (1340–1416) among the first to dress himself and his household in the new shade, and through the 1400s the courts of Europe borrowed the fruit's name for it [8]. The fruit itself was rising in status as the sweet orange from East Asia replaced the bitter one, and an orangery became a sign of wealth [8]. From the sixteenth century, American dyewoods kept orange in fashion, mostly as small touches beside the reds, blues and blacks of rich dress [8].

Science took longer. The Jesuit François d'Aguilon, in 1613, ranked orange with green and purple as a mixed color, made from the three middle ones [8]. Newton is usually credited with giving orange its place: he first named five colors in the spectrum and then, in 1671–72, added orange and [[indigo]] [11][12]. The seven are not natural divisions of the spectrum. Newton wanted seven to match the notes of the musical scale, and he admitted the division was artificial [11][13].

Studies of language tell the same story of a late arrival. Berlin and Kay's 1969 survey placed orange among the last basic color terms a language acquires, alongside [[purple]], [[pink]] and grey [13]. Critics say the scheme is overstated, especially in popular retellings [13][45]. During the First World War the chemist Wilhelm Ostwald even dropped the French loanwords *orange* and *violet* from his German color system, coining *Kress* and *Veil* instead [14].

sections.title: Dyeing orange
sections.body:
Before synthetic dyes, an orange cloth was usually a red dye pushed toward yellow or a yellow pushed toward red. [[madder|Madder]] fixed with alum gives an orange-red rather than a pink [15]. Safflower gives yellow in an alkaline bath and a crimson pink in an acid one, with orange- and pink-leaning yellows in between [15][9]. It was so often sold in place of saffron that it earned the name bastard saffron [15]. The Incas took orange from annatto seeds [17], and Hebridean weavers took it from peat soot [19].

The weakness of these dyes shaped a national flag. The Dutch flag began as orange, white and blue, after the livery of William I, but no orange dye would hold: the stripe faded to yellow or darkened to red, and by the 1660s it had been changed to red [2].

Finlay's chapter on orange is, fittingly, about a finish rather than a fabric. She follows the orange-brown varnish of Cremona violins and the materials that may have colored it, from madder to dragon's blood and mastic [15]. Stradivari's varnish recipe was lost around 1750, and luthiers still argue about it [15].

sections.title: The House of Orange
sections.body:
Orange became political in the later sixteenth century as the color of the princes of Orange, who led the largely Protestant northern Netherlands against Spain [8]. William I, the prince who led the revolt, was shot at the Prinsenhof on 10 July 1584 [2]. In a portrait of 1579 he wears black trimmed with orange and gold embroidery [2].

When the Dutch retook New York on 20 July 1673, they renamed it New Orange; the name lasted less than a year, St Clair says, before the city was ceded to the English in 1674 [2]. The flag of New York City still carries an orange stripe [2]. In Ireland, orange stands for the Protestant community and green for the Catholic one, with white between them on the flag [8]. A Boer republic in South Africa was the Orange Free State [1].

Carrots are a smaller thread in the story. Before the seventeenth century they were usually purple or yellow, and over the next hundred years Dutch growers bred orange varieties [2]. St Clair tells this inside the House of Orange story, but none of these books shows that the growers meant to honor the princes [2].

sections.title: Orange in the paintbox
sections.body:
For most of history painters had no good pure orange. Mixing red and yellow costs brightness, because each pigment absorbs some of the orange light the other reflects, and George Field argued for single-pigment oranges for that reason [20]. Ball puts it plainly: until the nineteenth century there was no good, pure orange pigment, and no violet either [20].

The natural oranges were dangerous. Realgar is an orange-red arsenic sulfide, about 70 per cent arsenic [27], and Egyptian painters already ground it [21]. Cennino Cennini, who called the yellow [[orpiment]] poisonous, warned that realgar was worse [16]. Ball calls realgar the only true orange of the Renaissance, available in Venice from about 1490 [22]. Titian used it for the cymbal player's orange in *[[art:commons-Q1206860|Bacchus and Ariadne]]* [22], and Veronese's oranges hold both realgar and pararealgar, a second crystal form of the same compound [42]. Even so, realgar was only ever used sparingly [42].

Red lead, or minium, was the cheap orange-red. It is yellower than [[vermilion]], Pliny called it flame-colored, and the *miniator* who painted manuscript capitals with it gave English the word miniature [3].

The first strong, pure orange came with chromium. Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin isolated the metal in 1797 from crocoite, an orange mineral from a Siberian gold mine first described in 1762 [43][5]. He described orange lead chromate in 1809 [26]. Precipitated from an alkaline solution, lead chromate comes out orange, and Ball counts chrome orange as the first pure, strong orange artists ever had [23]. By 1835 Field could list two chrome oranges, one made with lead and one with mercury [26].

Cadmium followed. Friedrich Stromeyer found the metal in 1817 in the waste of a zinc works, and its sulfide comes out yellow or orange depending on the size of its grains [23]. Gage notes that cadmium yellow-orange was not generally available to artists until the 1840s [28]. Today a tube labelled [[cadmium-orange]] may hold no cadmium at all: many such paints use organic pigments, and the name now describes a hue rather than a recipe [25].

sections.title: Orange against blue
sections.body:
Painters paired orange with [[blue]] long before theory explained it. In 1535 the Venetian Fulvio Pellegrini Morato listed blue with orange among the most beautiful pairings [30]. In a draft for the *Opticks* in the 1690s, Newton noted that painters set gold on blue [12]. In 1772 the entomologist Ignaz Schiffermüller drew a color circle that put blue directly opposite orange [29].

The Impressionists made the pair a signature, setting bright chrome and cadmium oranges against blues [1]. Monet's *Impression, Sunrise* is built around a small orange sun [1]. Margaret Livingstone measured it: the sun is no lighter than the grey clouds around it, so the part of vision that tracks lightness barely registers it, and it seems to shimmer [32]. Renoir's *Boating on the Seine* (1879–80) sets a skiff of thick, nearly unmixed chrome orange against cobalt-blue water [24].

Seurat went further and gave sunlight itself a color, adding dots of what he called solar orange among his greens [24]. The popular idea that such dots mix in the eye into something brighter is not borne out: Ball notes that small dots of complementary colors tend to add up to grey [24].

Which color counts as orange's opposite depends on the system. On the painter's red-yellow-blue wheel it is blue; on screens and in afterimages, blue sits opposite yellow instead [31]. Kandinsky, for his part, compared orange to a man sure of his own strength [44].

sections.title: Robes, flags and warnings
sections.body:
In India and Southeast Asia orange is a sacred color in Hinduism and Buddhism, and thought to bring luck [8]. The monks' robes called saffron were rarely dyed with saffron, which was too costly and too fugitive. In Tibet robes were usually dyed with turmeric, and in Thailand with jackfruit heartwood [16]. The [[deep-saffron]] band of India's 1947 flag was explained as standing for renunciation [4].

In the West, orange became the color of being seen [8]. It shows at night and in fog, so it marks life jackets, buoys, building sites and toxic labels [8]. Against blue-grey asphalt it stands out even in low light, and aircraft flight recorders, the black boxes, are painted orange so they can be found [1]. Faber Birren's 1944 safety code, drawn up with du Pont, gave orange to cutting and crushing hazards [36], and the American ANSI standard uses it for moderate risk, between red and yellow [37]. Fluorescent Day-Glo orange returns more orange light than falls on it, by re-emitting shorter wavelengths as longer ones [33].

Irving Morrow chose the Golden Gate Bridge's international orange in 1935, to blend with the hills and stand out against sea and sky [1]. Penguin Books took the color from 1935 [6], and Hermès boxes turned orange in the Second World War because it was the last paperboard color available [1]. Pastoureau records that the orange and apple-green estates of the 1960s and 1970s drew petitions from residents asking for white or grey [8]. In 2004 the protests that followed a fraudulent presidential election in Ukraine became the Orange Revolution [8]. Do not confuse any of these with [[international-orange-engineering]], a name for a deep red-orange.

sections.title: Orange light, brown paint
sections.body:
Most of the orange people see is light rather than paint. Candle flame is about 2,000 kelvin and an incandescent bulb about 3,000, both far warmer than daylight at about 6,500 [34]. At sunset, larger dust and salt particles in the air leave the orange and red ends of the light to reach the eye [18].

Orange light that is dimmed stays orange, but orange paint darkened with black turns brown [35]. Ball points out the oddity: a dim blue is still called blue, but a dim yellow or orange needs a new word, brown [20]. That gives one way to train the eye. Look at a [[terracotta]] pot half in sun and half in shade, and watch the same surface move from orange to brown.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a screen color within six units of this orange covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only 16 works [39]. Where it does appear it is mostly Indian: Rajput court painting carries it 46 times as often as the archive average (3 of 97 works), and Pahari painting 25 times (2 of 118) [39]. The work where it covers the most canvas is a Rajput *Maru Ragini* page of about 1650, at 31 per cent of the surface [39]. The earliest dated example is the Master of Heiligenkreuz's *Death of Saint Clare*, of about 1400 [39].

The surprise is what is missing. Of the 140 paintings tagged Impressionist in the archive, not one has this orange over five per cent of its canvas [39]. Their oranges are strokes and accents, too small to show at that threshold [39]. Across the 16 works where it does appear, it never sits among the shadows: 62 per cent of the time it falls in the middle lightness range and 38 per cent among the highlights [39]. Van Gogh's *[[art:nga-164923|Still Life of Oranges and Lemons with Blue Gloves]]*, as photographed, has no orange among its six largest colors; the nearest is a dark goldenrod [39]. Jac van Looij's *[[art:rijks-20028212|Orange Festival]]* reads as browns and one brick red [39].

These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test [39]. The swatch here is a strong orange. The CSS keyword `orange` is much yellower, about 15 units away, and `darkorange` about 6.5 [40]. Our nearest named neighbors, all within four units, are Heat Wave, Pastel Orange, [[pumpkin]] and [[cadmium-orange]]; [[tangerine]] is just under five [40]. In Google Books the word, fruit and color together, peaks around 1900 and stays above 60 per cent of that level from 1800 on [41].

questions.q: Why did European painters before about 1800 so rarely use a pure, bright orange?
choices: There was no good pure orange pigment: mixtures of red and yellow lost brightness, and realgar was a poisonous arsenic compound
The Church banned orange in religious paintings
Orange was reserved by law for the House of Orange
Orange paint turned green in oil
questions.answer: There was no good pure orange pigment: mixtures of red and yellow lost brightness, and realgar was a poisonous arsenic compound

questions.q: True or false: Newton listed orange as one of seven natural bands he found in the spectrum.
A terracotta pot is orange in the sun. What do we usually call the same surface in deep shade?

openers: Before the 1500s English had no word for orange: people said yellow-red.
In 1673 the Dutch renamed New York New Orange. The name lasted less than a year.
Look at a terracotta pot half in shade: dim orange is what we call brown.

issues: New Orange duration kept but attributed to St Clair ('less than 12 months'); the card itself only gives 1673 and 1674.
Verified against books: Newton five-then-seven, 1502 vs 1512, realgar/chrome orange, Morrow/Golden Gate, kelvin figures, Impressionist and Seurat claims; no myth-list item asserted as fact.
